overview: This map’s Armenia represents part of the region during caliphal rule, not a restored Armenian kingdom. Dvin served as a caliphal governor’s seat until 789. The imported outline covers a northern and eastern slice: Talin is inside it, while Dvin is just outside. The map’s “Sasanian E” alias is misleading for this period; neither the outline nor its 700 to 800 interval defines the whole historical province.

periods.title: Umayyad rule and Armenian princes
periods.summary: Caliphal governors and Armenian lords negotiated authority in a larger province called Arminiya. Conflict and rebellion accompanied those arrangements.

periods.title: Abbasid rule and rebellion
periods.summary: The Abbasid era brought further confrontations, culminating in the unsuccessful Armenian revolt of 774 to 775.

periods.title: Changing fortunes, continuing communities
periods.summary: After the revolt, regional society continued. Ghewond’s history follows political events into the later 780s.

items.text: Armenian princes still mattered under outside rule. Ghewond describes governor Marwan appointing Ashot Bagratuni as presiding prince in the 730s. Ashot then sought overdue cavalry pay from Caliph Hisham: political cooperation involved money for mounted soldiers as well as titles.

Christian Armenian communities belonged to the caliphate’s protected but subordinate non-Muslim population. Church life could continue, while liability for the jizya poll tax marked an unequal legal position. Religious protection did not mean equal citizenship in the modern sense.

Power also rested on family estates. The Kamsarakans held principalities in Shirak and Arsharunik. Following a failed late eighth-century revolt, they sold these lands to the Bagratids. A dynasty could lose its regional power without its descendants or cultural connections disappearing.

sections.title: Everyday objects and practical water supplies

items.text: Dvin’s excavated pottery, broadly dated to the fifth through eighth centuries, includes jars, pitchers, cups and small perfume containers. These reveal different jobs for different vessels: storing, pouring, drinking and keeping a small valuable liquid. A kitchen cupboard already needed more than one shape.

Oil lamps and an inkpot appear among Dvin’s broadly dated fifth- to eighth-century finds. Lighting a room and writing required physical equipment, not just skill. An excavated object can preserve a small working detail that a story about kings leaves out.

Glass vessels also survive from fifth- to eighth-century Dvin. Their fragments widen the household picture beyond clay: people used different materials for containers. This evidence identifies objects, without telling us that every family could afford the same possessions.

The Dvin excavation report identifies water mains as part of a complex urban water-supply system in its fifth- to eighth-century material. Moving water through a town required planned infrastructure. These remains do not establish that every home had a tap or a toilet.

sections.title: Talin: two brothers, a cathedral and an inscription

items.text: At Talin, monk Uxtaytur and his brother Tuti endowed the cathedral with a water source. Their inscription dates the gift to Armenian year 232, corresponding to 15 May 783 through 13 May 784. Here, family cooperation left a particularly practical monument.

The donors protected their gift with a written curse against anyone who destroyed the water source. An ordinary “please do not break this” sign apparently did not feel strong enough. The warning tied damage to spiritual responsibility for the donor’s sins.

Talin’s cathedral was probably built in the later seventh century, so it already had a history by the time of the water gift. Black and red tufa stone formed its walls; surviving painted decoration includes an open book resting on a cushioned throne.

Written Armenian: ՏՈՒՏԻ ԵՂԲԱՅՐ ԻՄ ,  Tuti ełbayr im, “Tuti, my brother.” This is a modern scholarly transcription of three surviving words in line 3 of Talin’s water inscription, dated 783/784. The family relationship is recorded on stone, not supplied by a modern storyteller.

sections.title: Learning, books and food in a mathematics lesson

items.text: A useful earlier background is the seventh-century scholar Anania of Shirak. His autobiography describes eight years studying with Tychikos at Trebizond. The teacher could translate Greek into Armenian and owned scientific, historical and medical books: education crossed linguistic and political boundaries.

Anania’s arithmetic gives food a starring role. Its seventh-century problems involve garden lettuce, river fish and wine measured into jars. These are imaginary exercises built around recognizable activities, preserved in later manuscripts; they are glimpses of a teaching world rather than a menu for every Armenian household.

One problem has a student bringing apples to his teacher. Three groups of jesters successively take three-quarters of the remaining fruit. Only five apples arrive. Working backward gives 320 at the start: a surprisingly expensive mathematics lesson, at least in apples!

The same arithmetic collection includes entertaining puzzles intended for social gatherings. Fractions and number tricks could be a form of amusement as well as instruction. This is evidence for the book’s purpose, not a claim that every eighth-century dinner came with a compulsory mathematics quiz.

Ghewond wrote in the late eighth century, drawing on older informants and events closer to his own lifetime. His Christian outlook and Bagratid patronage shaped the story. The surviving manuscript tradition is later, so his text is neither a neutral government report nor an original eighth-century notebook.

Dvin became a major archaeological project in the twentieth century, with excavations running from 1937 apart from the wartime interruption. Much of the uncovered material belongs to later centuries. Dating each find matters: an impressive medieval ruin cannot automatically describe life in the year 700.

ending.text: The map’s cutoff at 800 is not the disappearance of Armenian society. Dvin’s role as the caliphal governor’s seat had ended in 789, but the city continued through later struggles involving Arab rulers and Armenian dynasties. This card’s century is one phase within that longer history.
